desc: Prove the greedy/criterion: K pairs feasible in [L,R] ⟺ for all x in [0,K): 2*A[L+x] ≤ A[R-K+1+x] (K-smallest vs K-largest rearrangement argument), monotone in K, with K ≤ m/2 ensuring disjointness.

Reduce criterion to static RMQ: K feasible ⟺ max w over [L, L+K-1] ≤ m-K, where w[i] = nxt[i]-i and nxt[i] = first index with A ≥ 2*A[i]; verified by hand against all of sample 1 and every query of sample 2.

Design fast answering: O(N) two-pointer for nxt, O(N log N) max sparse table on w (list-of-lists, ~35MB since max() reuses int objects), per query O(log N) binary lifting with running-max trick using st[b][L+K] directly (no per-step bit_length/second lookup).

Edge-case analysis: INF = N for missing nxt (always exceeds d ≤ N-1); w[i] ≥ 1 so cur=0 works as -inf; duplicates handled (strict 2*top ≤ bottom via ≥ in lower_bound); m=2/K=0 cases verified on samples.

Implement the full solution: compute w[i] = nxt[i]-i via two pointers (nxt[i] = first index with A[j] ≥ 2*A[i], INF if none), build a max sparse table over w, and answer each query by binary-lifting K from 0 with the running-max trick (cand = max(cur, st[b][L+K]); feasible iff cand ≤ m-(K+2^b)); validate against both samples.
Brute-force-verify the implemented query answer against exhaustive matching on small random arrays (all intervals) to guard against off-by-one errors in the 0-indexed RMQ bounds.
Final performance pass: fast I/O via sys.stdin.buffer.read().split(), confirmed ~O((N+Q) log N) runtime with small constant (~2.5s total estimate) and ~30MB memory; solution finalized.
